# Fenwick says staff could identify instruments awaiting parts

For new jobs, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use but postponed adding its backlog. This fictional case shows workshop managers the setup choices and the limits of the evidence.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Jobs awaiting parts and those ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets before the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule in January 2026.

## The team shapes the setup

The team chose Benchline after checking it could distinguish the two statuses. The workshop defined them and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Customer collection arrangements continued to be discussed by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained what the team had to settle: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary sets limits on the findings

The trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale reflects on the choice

In the same email interview, Vale said: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source-comparison report: draft 1

Compared the complete supplied brief and source package with the complete draft, including its title, introduction, byline, headings and quotations. Target language: British English. Both source and draft are English; no quotation translation is involved. General editing, mechanical review and length assessment are outside this report.

## Findings

### F1 — Source support: the title states a stronger result than the reported ability

**Draft:** “Fenwick staff see which instruments await parts”

**Source:** “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” The source additionally qualifies the evidential position: “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

**Difference:** The source attributes an ability to the trial summary: staff *could see* which instruments were waiting for parts. The title makes a direct assertion that staff *see* them. It does not carry the modal qualification or the source of the reported experience. The historical present may be a normal headline convention; this finding does not depend on treating that convention alone as a defect.

**Concrete case, source true but draft assertion false:** The summary reports that the schedule enabled staff to identify instruments awaiting parts, but staff did not actually exercise that ability in ordinary job handling. A reported ability can hold without the observation asserted by “staff see” having occurred. Alternatively, the workshop's summary can report an ability that its writer believed existed, without that report independently establishing the actual result. No supplied statement rules out either case. The final source sentence expressly limits the package to reported experience.

**Reverse direction:** Actual seeing entails the ability to see, so there is no reverse counterexample to that modal relation. Nor can a material-compatible case erase the source report, because the supplied package expressly gives it. The defect is the stronger actuality and unqualified evidential position added to the source's attributed ability, not a mutually exclusive account.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick summary says staff could see which instruments awaited parts”. This preserves the visibility result while naming its source and retaining its modality.

### F2 — Source support: the introduction supplies an unsupported sequence

**Draft:** “After a six-week scheduling trial, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding its backlog.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Later: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The draft's introductory “After” places the approval and postponement after the six-week trial. The source gives the trial duration, summary date and decision, but supplies no date for the decision and no explicit ordering between that decision and the trial's completion. The subject change from the manager to Fenwick is a defensible institutional attribution in this context and is not a separate finding.

**Concrete case, source true but draft assertion false:** The manager approved continued use for new jobs and postponed adding the backlog in week five; the team completed the six-week trial, and the 23 February summary then recorded the decision. Every supplied statement remains true, but the decision did not occur after the trial. No supplied sentence excludes this case. Its position after the summary description in the material is not a stated chronology of the decision.

**Reverse direction:** A decision made after the trial is compatible with both accounts. There is no converse counterexample within the supplied material: the defect is the draft's narrowing of an unspecified decision date into a specified sequence.

**Smallest supported repair:** Delete “After a six-week scheduling trial,” and begin “Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use …”. The body already gives the six-week duration and preserves the status-review condition.

The two findings above are the only source-support defects identified. The following accounting covers all factual and attributed content. Source passages are quoted in their original English. Where wording changes are defensible, no finding is recorded.

### 1. Title: workshop staff and instruments awaiting parts

**Draft:** “Fenwick staff see which instruments await parts”.

**Source:** “It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” The antecedent is “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026”. The workshop is identified throughout as Fenwick Instrument Repairs.

“Fenwick staff” identifies the same workshop staff, and “await parts” names the same condition as “were waiting for parts”. No instrument type, count or gender is added. The change from an attributed ability to direct observation is F1. No causal claim about Benchline shortening repairs appears here.

### 2. Introduction: trial duration and chronology

**Draft:** “After a six-week scheduling trial”.

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.”

“Scheduling trial” is a concise description of the shared bench schedule trial. The six-week duration is exact. The introduced chronological relation is F2.

**Source:** “The manager approved continued use for new jobs”.

Neither version asserts completed implementation of the approved decision or a recommendation for other workshops. Apart from the introductory chronology in F2, there is no changed scope, modality or certainty.

### 4. Introduction: backlog postponement

**Source:** “but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions”.

The draft states the same postponement. It does not say the postponement was indefinite or for another reason. The body carries the source's status-review condition explicitly. “Its” identifies the workshop's backlog; the source's local context establishes that referent. The summary is defensible with that fuller qualification in the body. F2 covers only the added date relation.

# Fenwick staff see which instruments await parts

After a six-week scheduling trial, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding its backlog. This fictional case shows workshop managers the setup choices and the limits of the evidence.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Jobs awaiting parts and those ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets before the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule in January 2026.

## The team shapes the setup

The team chose Benchline after checking it could distinguish the two statuses. The workshop defined them and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Customer collection arrangements continued to be discussed by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained what the team had to settle: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary sets limits on the findings

The trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale reflects on the choice

In the same email interview, Vale said: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source-comparison report: draft 1

Compared the complete supplied brief and source package with the complete draft, including its title, introduction, byline, headings and quotations. Target language: British English. Both source and draft are English; no quotation translation is involved. General editing, mechanical review and length assessment are outside this report.

## Findings

### F1 — Source support: the title states a stronger result than the reported ability

**Draft:** “Fenwick staff see which instruments await parts”

**Source:** “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” The source additionally qualifies the evidential position: “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

**Difference:** The source attributes an ability to the trial summary: staff *could see* which instruments were waiting for parts. The title makes a direct assertion that staff *see* them. It does not carry the modal qualification or the source of the reported experience. The historical present may be a normal headline convention; this finding does not depend on treating that convention alone as a defect.

**Concrete case, source true but draft assertion false:** The summary reports that the schedule enabled staff to identify instruments awaiting parts, but staff did not actually exercise that ability in ordinary job handling. A reported ability can hold without the observation asserted by “staff see” having occurred. Alternatively, the workshop's summary can report an ability that its writer believed existed, without that report independently establishing the actual result. No supplied statement rules out either case. The final source sentence expressly limits the package to reported experience.

**Reverse direction:** Staff might see awaiting-parts instruments in the workshop by inspection while the summary never reports the schedule's visibility. That would satisfy the title's unqualified observation but not the source's specific reported finding. This is a difference in the propositions, rather than an assertion that such an alternative happened.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick summary says staff could see which instruments awaited parts”. This preserves the visibility result while naming its source and retaining its modality.

### F2 — Source support: the introduction supplies an unsupported sequence

**Draft:** “After a six-week scheduling trial, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding its backlog.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Later: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.”

**Difference:** The draft's introductory “After” places the approval and postponement after the six-week trial. The source gives the trial duration, summary date and decision, but supplies no date for the decision and no explicit ordering between that decision and the trial's completion. The subject change from the manager to Fenwick is a defensible institutional attribution in this context and is not a separate finding.

**Concrete case, source true but draft assertion false:** The manager approved continued use for new jobs and postponed adding the backlog in week five; the team completed the six-week trial, and the 23 February summary then recorded the decision. Every supplied statement remains true, but the decision did not occur after the trial. No supplied sentence excludes this case. Its position after the summary description in the material is not a stated chronology of the decision.

**Reverse direction:** A decision made after the trial is compatible with both accounts. There is no converse counterexample within the supplied material: the defect is the draft's narrowing of an unspecified decision date into a specified sequence.

**Smallest supported repair:** Delete “After a six-week scheduling trial,” and begin “Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use …”. The body already gives the six-week duration and preserves the status-review condition. Alternatively, “Fenwick Instrument Repairs ran a six-week scheduling trial and approved continued use …” avoids an explicit after-trial claim.

The summary is defensible with that fuller qualification in the body. F2 covers only the added date relation.

# Fenwick staff see which instruments await parts

After a six-week scheduling trial, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding its backlog. This fictional case shows workshop managers the setup choices and the limits of the evidence.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Jobs awaiting parts and those ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets before the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule in January 2026.

## The team shapes the setup

The team chose Benchline after checking it could distinguish the two statuses. The workshop defined them and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Customer collection arrangements continued to be discussed by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained what the team had to settle: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary sets limits on the findings

The trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale reflects on the choice

In the same email interview, Vale said: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’

# Source-comparison report: draft 1

Compared the complete supplied brief and source package with the complete draft, including its title, introduction, byline, headings and quotations. Target language: British English. Both source and draft are English; no quotation translation is involved. General editing, mechanical review and length assessment are outside this report.

## Findings

### F1 — Source support: the title states a stronger result than the reported ability

**Draft:** “Fenwick staff see which instruments await parts”

**Source:** “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.” The source additionally qualifies the evidential position: “The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop.”

**Difference:** The source attributes an ability to the trial summary: staff *could see* which instruments were waiting for parts. The title makes a direct assertion that staff *see* them. It does not carry the modal qualification or the source of the reported experience. The historical present may be a normal headline convention; this finding does not depend on treating that convention alone as a defect.

**Concrete case, source true but draft assertion false:** The summary reports that the schedule enabled staff to identify instruments awaiting parts, but staff did not actually exercise that ability in ordinary job handling. A reported ability can hold without the observation asserted by “staff see” having occurred. Alternatively, the workshop's summary can report an ability that its writer believed existed, without that report independently establishing the actual result. No supplied statement rules out either case. The final source sentence expressly limits the package to reported experience.

**Reverse direction:** Staff might see awaiting-parts instruments in the workshop by inspection while the summary never reports the schedule's visibility. That would satisfy the title's unqualified observation but not the source's specific reported finding. This is a difference in the propositions, rather than an assertion that such an alternative happened.

**Smallest supported repair:** “Fenwick summary says staff could see which instruments awaited parts”. This preserves the visibility result while naming its source and retaining its modality.

### F2 — Source support: the introduction supplies an unsupported sequence

**Draft:** “After a six-week scheduling trial, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding its backlog.”

**Source:** “In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule.” Later: “The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. **Concrete case, source true but draft assertion false:** The manager approved continued use for new jobs and postponed adding the backlog in week five; the team completed the six-week trial, and the 23 February summary then recorded the decision. # Fenwick says staff could identify instruments awaiting parts

For new jobs, Fenwick Instrument Repairs approved continued use but postponed adding its backlog. This fictional case shows workshop managers the setup choices and the limits of the evidence.

By Thomas Barregren

Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments. Jobs awaiting parts and those ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets before the team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule in January 2026.

## The team shapes the setup

The team chose Benchline after checking it could distinguish the two statuses. The workshop defined them and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session. Customer collection arrangements continued to be discussed by telephone.

In an email interview on 2 March 2026, manager Priya Vale explained what the team had to settle: ‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’

## The summary sets limits on the findings

The trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts.

The summary does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction. The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions.

## Vale reflects on the choice

In the same email interview, Vale said: ‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’
